title: Greek Heroes
subtitle: Excellence, cleverness, cost, and competing versions

suggestedTopics.title: Anger, honor, and consequence
suggestedTopics.description: Follow how the Iliad turns Achilles’ injured honor into a story about cost, grief, and responsibility.
suggestedTopics.prompt: Track how Achilles’ anger changes from Book 1 through Patroclus’ death and Priam’s visit.

suggestedTopics.title: Cunning, names, and disguise
suggestedTopics.description: Explore how Odysseus survives through intelligence, false names, patience, and recognition scenes.
suggestedTopics.prompt: Compare the Cyclops episode with the recognition scenes back on Ithaca.

suggestedTopics.title: When heroic stories change
suggestedTopics.description: Use later mythography and biography to see how heroic genealogies and adventures are reorganized.
suggestedTopics.prompt: Ask which source tells the version, when it was written, and what kind of work it is.

suggestedTopics.title: Heroes on the tragic stage
suggestedTopics.description: Prepare for later lessons on how Athenian drama reshapes heroic traditions into conflict, suffering, and debate.
suggestedTopics.prompt: Look for where a tragedy chooses one version and sharpens its moral or political conflict.

assessment.title: Greek Heroes assessment
assessment.prompt: Five new questions revisit the week’s events, interpretations, and source distinctions. Taking the assessment completes the week; missed answers remain practice priorities.

question.prompt: How do the two openings differ in what they foreground?

choices.text: The Iliad begins with the Argo while the Odyssey begins with Theseus.
The Iliad names anger and loss; the Odyssey names travel, suffering, and return.
Both openings describe the same battle scene.

question.explanation: The Iliad's invocation foregrounds Achilles' anger; the Odyssey's invocation foregrounds a journey and its costs.

question.prompt: After the heralds take Briseis, where does Achilles go and whom does he call?

choices.text: He goes to the seashore and calls on Thetis.
He sails to Crete and calls on Ariadne.
He goes to Mount Oeta and calls on Zeus.

question.explanation: Book 1 says Achilles goes alone to the sea and prays to his mother Thetis.

question.prompt: What does the Odyssey say Odysseus suffers while trying to save his men?

choices.text: He loses his armor in the Nemean cave.
He is trapped by the suitors in Ithaca.
Much suffering by sea, and he cannot save his crew.

question.explanation: Butler's invocation says Odysseus suffers by sea and cannot save his men.

question.prompt: Why keep Apollonius and Euripides distinct?

choices.text: One is an eyewitness translation of the other.
Their genres and narrative settings shape different presentations of Medea.

question.explanation: Their genres and narrative settings shape different presentations of Medea. is the passage-specific answer. Check The Argonautica (Argonautica 3, Medea gives Jason the charm); The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I (Medea, Nurse's prologue), keeping each work and version distinct.

question.prompt: What is a responsible claim about Plutarch’s Theseus?

choices.text: Plutarch records his personal meeting with Theseus.
Theseus wrote Plutarch’s account of Athens.
Plutarch presents a legendary founder through later biography.

question.explanation: Plutarch presents a legendary founder through later biography. is the passage-specific answer. Check Bibliotheca (Library) (Library 2.4.12, oracle assigns service); Plutarch: Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans (Life of Theseus, civic unification), keeping each work and version distinct.
